          STORIES & ORAL HERITAGE · AFRICAN CONNECTIONS

          Ananse across the Atlantic: African voices, Jamaican transformations

          Hear an African-language telling and Ghanaian community voices, then compare them with Jamaican versions without flattening either tradition.

          ← Storytelling collectionAfrican voices & film →

          Start with Akan places and people

          “From Africa” is a beginning, not a complete provenance. Anansi's connection with Akan storytelling, including the Asante of present-day Ghana, is identified in Jamaica's institutional accounts and in scholarship. Africa is a continent of many languages and narrative traditions. A Ghanaian Ananse story should not become evidence that every African community tells the same tales. [2]

          The route to Jamaica includes the forced movement of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. What travelled was knowledge carried by people: stories, patterns of performance and possibilities for making new versions. The connection does not require an unchanged script. Jamaican teller, audience, language and circumstances could alter a story while retaining a recognizable trickster or narrative problem. Zobel Marshall's study explicitly treats transformation as part of the history. [1]

          AKAN / GHANA

          Ananse in a living repertoire

          Hear a Twi telling and people from the Twifu Hemang area discussing the figure.

          JAMAICA

          Anancy in named Jamaican versions

          Read individual tellers, then hear Jamaican performers make the tradition their own.

          Hear an African-language telling

          The Twi-language Kwaku Ananse and the Pot of Wisdom is published on the channel identified by YouTube metadata as Kwabena Antwi-Boasiako. The recording does not separately name its narrator, so the uploader is credited as publisher rather than automatically assigned the voice. It is an Akan-language resource, not a Jamaican-dialect lesson. The source offers an English caption track; captions are supplied by the source, not translated by this guide. [6]

          A reading companion to the motif: Ananse tries to possess wisdom for himself, yet a child supplies an idea he has missed. A container that seems to hold everything cannot make its owner the only source of understanding. The Ghanaian scholars Emmanuel K. E. Antwi, Isaac F. Adjei and Joseph K. Asuming discuss a pot-of-wisdom narrative in their account of Akan ideas of wisdom. Their study compares these with Old Testament concepts while stressing differences. It does not establish an unchanged Jamaican version. [3]

          Open the African listening collection →

          Ghanaian communities speak about Ananse

          The filmmaker's description of Who is Kweku Ananse? identifies farmers, a herbalist, a paramount chief, former nurses and schoolchildren in the Twifu Hemang area of Ghana's Central Region. Kweku Kjei Donkoh and Johannes Preuß ask the questions. Community roles and a stated location give the discussion a social setting. It is documentary inquiry, rather than one disembodied voice authorized to speak for a continent. [4]

          The related Kweku Ananse and the Chest of Stories was produced near Kakum in 2013 and uploaded in 2016. It dramatizes an Ananse tale. Keep the two records separate: people discussing a character and performers making a film around him are not identical evidence. Both show that African storytelling has a present, rather than existing only as an origin chapter for Caribbean culture. [5]

          Read African authors as authors

          Ghanaian-born Adwoa Badoe's The Pot of Wisdom, illustrated by the Malian artist Baba Wagué Diakité, offers ten Ananse tales. The publisher provides an excerpt and identifies their creative roles. Follow that edition as a work by particular African artists, rather than replacing their telling with an unattributed internet summary. Read the publisher's excerpt and edition details → [7]

          Rattray's 1930 Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales is another historical reading route. Its institutional catalogue explicitly credits African illustrators, but Rattray is the collector and translator. A colonial-era printed collection is not the unmediated speech of all Akan people. We link the record for study without pretending to have consulted its whole contents or silently importing its translations into our Jamaican tales. [8]

          Compare versions without forcing a match

          Put the wisdom-pot story beside Henry Spence's Turtle's Escape. Both unsettle the idea that Anansi alone controls intelligence. Their actions and stakes differ: a monopoly over knowledge in one, a threat of being eaten in the other. This is a thematic comparison chosen by the guide. It does not establish that Spence's tale descended from that precise Ghanaian recording or that the two tellers shared one moral.

          Next compare the ownership of stories in the Ghanaian film with Bird Arinto, where a claim to someone else's achievement is exposed. Ask who controls public recognition and what evidence overturns a claim. Similar questions can illuminate two stories without making them interchangeable. Note what is absent as carefully as what resembles: a character, a song, a reward or an audience response.

          The African connection is not an accent effect

          The point of listening is to encounter people using their languages and expressive resources. An “African-sounding” narrator with no known connection to a tradition supplies no such provenance. The collection separates the Twi upload, Ghanaian community interviews and film. It adds no synthetic narration and asks no one to imitate either African or Jamaican speech.

          Tony's Call Follow the connection through people, places and versions. Africa is a continuing source of voices and scholarship, not a decorative label attached to a Jamaican tale.

          Scholarship & sources

          1. Zobel Marshall, E. (2012). Anansi's journey. UWI Press. Publisher description and contents consulted; full book not accessed.
          2. Jamaica Information Service. (2016). The origin of Anancy/Nancy stories. Akan connections, forced migration and Jamaican telling.
          3. Antwi, E. K. E., Adjei, I. F., & Asuming, J. K. (2020). Understanding wisdom in the Old Testament through its Akan (Ghana) parallels: Linkages and disconnections. Old Testament Essays, 33(3). Open article, especially the Akan wisdom discussion and pot narrative.
          4. JP DocFilm. (2012). Who is Kweku Ananse? Part 1. Producer identifies Twifu Hemang-area community interviewees and interviewers.
          5. JP DocFilm. (2016 upload). Kweku Ananse and the Chest of Stories. Producer describes the Ghana location and 2013 production; modern film adaptation.
          6. Antwi-Boasiako, K., publisher. Anansesem: Kwaku Ananse and the Pot of Wisdom (Twi). Upload metadata and caption-track inventory consulted. Narrator not separately identified.
          7. Badoe, A. The pot of wisdom: Ananse stories. Illustrated by Baba Wagué Diakité. Groundwood Books. Publisher account, African creator biographies and excerpt access; full book not reproduced.

          STORIES & ORAL HERITAGE

          Beyond Anancy: magical households, birds, riddles and warning tales

          The repertoire is wider than one spider. Songs carry warnings, children expose false claims and riddles turn everyday work into interpretation.

          ← Storytelling collectionComplete written tales →

          The spider does not own every role

          The phrase “Anansi story” can name a storytelling repertoire as well as a plot in which Anansi appears. Beckwith notes that the label was used broadly for storytelling, riddling and song in the communities she visited. Her collection gives a useful invitation: keep listening when a bird, an ordinary child or a mysterious visitor takes the centre of the account. [1]

          Birds, sound and evidence

          In The Golden Cage, the printed page places a short account of a king's daughter beside bird-song words. The song is part of the record we read, rather than background music added by this guide. In Bird Arinto, a boy's song helps him manage a threat; the tongue later provides evidence against a false claim. Neither tale needs to be an actual historical event to be worthy of attention.

          Ask what the song changes. Does it reveal something a powerful character wants hidden? Does it call another being closer, create delay or preserve a warning? Those are reading questions, not a universal explanation of Jamaican song. Each tale gives a different answer. Written syllables cannot reconstruct every detail of a historical performance.

          Magic households and dangerous hospitality

          Thomas White's The Tree-wife gives a household a magical origin and lets a voice follow a trail. Alfred Williams's The Barking Puppy makes a warning persist after the warning animal is destroyed. The latter includes graphic cruelty and a violent ending; it belongs in our darker-reading category. Calling both harmless bedtime stories would misdescribe the page.

          Folktale, legend and oral history also ask different questions. A tale can arrange impossible events to examine human conduct. A person's memory of a particular event has another relationship to evidence. The ACIJ/Jamaica Memory Bank collects across these areas, but their presence in one institution does not make them the same genre. Keep the teller, setting and kind of claim attached to the record. [2]

          Riddling belongs beside narrative

          Simeon Falconer's Settling the Father's Debt turns apparently impossible answers into explanations drawn from household life: borrowing, selling, illness and bodily discomfort. The listener has to reinterpret what has been said. That is a different pleasure from waiting for Anansi to reveal his plan, though both reward close attention to language.

          Try stopping before the explanations. Let a listener offer an interpretation, then return to Falconer's version. A wrong guess is not evidence that someone lacks cultural knowledge; the wording deliberately hides its reference. In her preface, Beckwith describes riddling as a social pastime in which people took turns proposing puzzles.

          A household collection of your own

          Ask a relative which version they remember, who told it, where the telling happened and whether it included a song. With permission, record their own words rather than prescribing how Jamaican they should sound. Keep the date, their preferred name, language and any limits on sharing. A family recollection is worth preserving even if it differs from a published version.

          When a story changes in your retelling, name the change. You might shorten an episode, soften a frightening ending or move the scene to a place a child knows. Those can be worthwhile choices. They become misleading when the result is passed off as the exact words of a named historical teller. This collection lets the historical text and your response remain visible together.

          Tony's Call Keep the laughter, the puzzle and the unsettling parts in view. Give ordinary people, birds, songs and magical households room beside Brer Anancy.

          JAMAICAN STORYTELLING · HISTORICAL SOURCE

          The Fish-basket.

          A stolen catch becomes a contest between physical force and deception.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: George Parkes, Mandeville.

          Reading note: Threats, killing and an animal death.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          One great hungry time. Anansi couldn’t get anyt’ing to eat, so he take up his hand-basket an’ a big pot an’ went down to the sea-side to catch fish. When he reach there, he make up a large fire and put the pot on the fire, an’ say, “Come, big fish!” He catch some big fish put them aside. He said, “Big fish go, make little fish come!” He then catch the little fish. He say, “Little fish go, make big fish come!” an’ say, “Big fish go, make little fish come!” He then catch the pot full an’ his hand-basket. He bile the pot full and sit down and eat it off; he then started home back with the pot on his head and the basket. Reaching a little way, he hide the pot away in the bush an take the basket along with him now.

          While going along, he meet up Tiger. Now Tiger is a very rough man an’ Anansi ’fraid of him. Tiger said to him, “What you have in that basket, sah?”—speak to him very rough. Anansi speak in a very feeble voice, say, “Nothing, sah! nothing, sah!” So both of them pass each other, an’ when they went on a little way, Tiger hide in the bush watching Anansi. Anansi then sit down underneath a tree, open his basket, take out the fishes one one, and say, “Pretty little yallah-tail this!” an’ put it aside; he take out a snapper an’ say, “Pretty little snapper this!” an’ put it one side; he take out a jack-fish an’ say, “Pretty little jack-fish!” an’ put it one side. Tiger then run up an’ say, “Think you havn’t not’ing in that basket, sah!” Anansi say, “I jus’ going down to the sea have a bathe, sah, an’ I catch them few ’itte fishes.” Tiger say, “Give it to me here, sah!”—talk in a very rough manner. An’ Tiger take it an’ eat them all an’ spit up the bones. Anansi then take up the bones an’ eat them, an’ while eating he grumble an’ say, “But look me bwoy labor do!” Tiger say, “What you say?” Anansi say, “Fly humbug me face, sah!” (brushing his face).

          So both of them start to go home now with the empty basket, but this time Anansi was studying for Tiger. When he reach part of the way, Anansi see a fruit-tree. Anansi say, “What a pretty fruit-tree!” (looking up in the tree). Tiger say, “Climb it, sah!” (in a rough manner). So when Anansi go up an’ pull some of the fruit, at that time Tiger was standing underneath the tree. Anansi look down on Tiger head an’ said, “Look lice in a Brar Tiger head!” Tiger said, “Come down an’ ketch it, sah!” Anansi come down an’ said to Tiger he kyan’t ketch it without he lean on the tree. Tiger said, “Lean on the tree, sah!” The hair on Tiger head is very long. So while Anansi ketchin’ the lice, Tiger fell asleep. Anansi now take the hair an’ lash it round the tree tie up Tiger on the tree. After he done that he wake up Tiger an’ say that he kyan’t ketch any more. Tiger in a rough manner say, “Come an’ ketch it, sah!” Anansi say, “I won’t!” So Anansi run off, Tiger spring after him, an’ fin’ out that his hair is tied on the tree. So Tiger say, “Come an’ loose me, sah!” Anansi say. “I won’t!” an’ Anansi sing now,

          “See how Anansi tie Tiger,

          See how Anansi tie Tiger,

          Tie him like a hog, Tiger,

          See how Anansi tie Tiger,

          Tie him like a hog, Tiger!”

          An’ Anansi leave him go home, an’ a hunter-man come an’ see Tiger tie on the tree, make kill him.

          Look again

          Who first takes someone else’s work, and how does the balance of power change?

          JAMAICAN STORYTELLING · HISTORICAL SOURCE

          The Storm.

          A storm warning gets Tiger tied to his own mango tree.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Vivian Bailey, Mandeville.

          Reading note: Deception and rough treatment.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Brer Tiger got a mango-tree in his place. Brer Nansi go an’ ask if he could sell him a ha’ penny wort’ of mango. Brer Tiger say no. Brer Nansi well want de mango. Brer Nansi say, “Law pass dat eb’ry man have tree mus’ tie on it ’cause going to get a heavy storm.” Brer Tiger say, well, mus’ tie him to de mango-tree. After Brer Nansi tie Tiger, climb up in de mango-tree, an’ eb’ry mango he eat tak it an’ lick Brer Tiger on de head. After he eat done, he shake off all de ripe mango an’ pick dem up go away leave Brer Tiger tie up on de mango-tree.

          Brer Tiger see Brer But pass an’ ask Brer But to loose him. Brer But say dat he kyan’t stop. Brer Tiger see Brer Ant passing, ask Brer Ant to loose him; Brer Ant say he kyan’t depon haste. Brer Tiger see Brer Duck-ants passing an’ ask him fe loose him. An’ don’ know if him will loose him, for don’ know if him will put up wid him slowness, for Duck-ants is a very slow man. After him loose him, Brer Tiger tell him many t’anks an’ tell him mus’ never let him hear any of Duck-ants’s frien’s pass him an’ don’ call up “How-dy-do.”

          Brer Nansi in a cotton tree were listening when dey talking. De nex’ evening, Brer Nansi go to Brer Tiger yard an’ knock at de door. An’ say, “Who is deah?” an’ say, “Mr. Duck-ants’s brudder.” An’ dey tak him in an’ mak much of him, get up tea because it was Mr. Duck-ants’s brudder, an’ after dat go to bed. In de morning provide tea for Mr. Duck-ants ’fore he wake, an’ when he wake an’ was washin’ his face he got to tak off his hat. An’ Brer Nansi is a man wid a bald head, an’ dey got to fin’ out it was Brer Nansi an’ dey run him out of de house.

          Look again

          Compare the warning with the danger in The Fish-basket. What makes each deception work?

          Tiger as Riding-horse.

          A boast about Tiger becomes a public demonstration.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: William Forbes, Dry River.

          Reading note: Humiliation and a song referring to death.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Tiger was walking to a yard an’ see two young misses, an’ he was courting one of de young misses. An’ as Anansi hear, Anansi go up to yard where de young misses is; an’ dey ax him said, “Mr. Anansi, you see Mr. Tiger?” An’ said, “O yes! I see Mr. Tiger, but I tell you, missus, Tiger is me fader ol’ ridin’-horse.” An’ when Tiger come to misses, dem tell him. An’ said him gwine Anansi, mak him come an’ prove witness befo’ him face how he is fader ol’ ridin’-horse!

          An’ when him come call Anansi, say, “Want you to come prove dis t’ing you say ’fore de misses,” Anansi say, “I nebber say so! but I kyan’ walk at all.” Tiger said, “If I hab to carry you ’pon me back, I will carry you go!” Anansi said, “Well, I wi’ go.” Anansi go tak out him saddle. Tiger say, “What you gwine do wid saddle?” Anansi say, “To put me foot down in de stirrup so when I gwine fall down, I weak, I can catch up.” An’ tak him bridle. Tiger say, “What you gwine do wid it?” Say, “Gwine put it in you mout’, when I gwine to fa’ down I can catch up.” Tiger say, “I don’ care what you do, mus’ put it on!” An’ him go back an’ tak horse-whip. An say, “Wha’ you gwine do wid de horse-whip?” An’ say, “Fe when de fly come, fan de fly.” An’ put on two pair of ’pur. An’ say, “Wha’ you gwine do wid ’pur?” An’ say, “If I don’ put on de ’pur, me foot wi’ cramp.” An’ come close to yard an’ close in wid de ’pur an’ horse-whip, an’ mak him gallop into de yard. An’ say, “Carry him in to stable, sah! I mak you to know what Anansi say true to de fac’, is me fader ol’ ridin’-horse.”

          Tiger tak to wood, Anansi sing a’ter him, “Po’ Tiger dead an’ gone!”

          Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na bom, Eb-ry-bod-y (?) Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na bom, (?) Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na. Po’ Ti-ger dead and gone, Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na, Eb-ry-bod-y go look fo’ dem wife, Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na, Eb-ry-bod-y go look fo’ dem wife, Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na, Si-lay-na bom.

          Tiger’s Breakfast.

          A breakfast trick is answered by a dangerous instruction.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains.

          Reading note: Food theft, bodily injury and animal cruelty.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          One day, Hanansi go Tiger house an’ eat breakfas’ every day, an’ tell Tiger, say, “Brar Tiger, to-morrow you mus’ come a my house; but when you hear me makin’ noise you mus’ come, for dat time breakfas’ is on, but when you hear me stay still you mustn’t come at all.” So when Tiger go, Hanansi eat done. And say, “Brar Tiger, you foot short!” Tiger say, “No, me no hear you mak noise!” Hanansi say, “No, so me said, for when man makin’ noise he kyan’ eat.” An’ say, “Well, nex’ day come back.” When Tiger come, Hanansi tak shame, gi’ him little breakfas’ but say, “Brar Tiger, when we go fe eat, when I say ‘Nyammy nyammy nyammy’ you mus’ say, ‘Nyam a wha’ eat’.” So Hanansi stay deh eat everyt’ing, Tiger never get one.

          Tiger study fe him. Nex’ day he go to Tiger yard. When Tiger gi’ him breakfast an’ gi’ him enough meat he said to Tiger, “Brar Tiger, a whe’ you get meat every day so?” Tiger said, “You know how me come by dis meat? When I see a cow lie down, I go up an’ run me han’ inside of de cow an’ hol’ de man tripe, so I never out of meat.” So Hanansi went his way an’ do de same. De cow frighten on de hill-side an’ turn head right down to lowland. Hanansi say, “Do, Brar Cow, don’t shut up me han’!” Cow fasten de han’ de better an’ gallop right down de hill an’ drag Hanansi over de stone. Dat’s de reason let you see Hanansi belly white.

          Look again

          When does the victim of one trick become the author of another?

          The Christening.

          Names of imaginary children conceal a disappearing shared meal.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Charles Wright, Maroon Town, Cock-pit country.

          Reading note: Theft and false accusation.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Anansi an’ Tiger bot’ of them fin’ one keg of butter. Anansi says to Tiger, “Let us hide it in the bushes.” Some days after, Anansi says to Tiger, “I receive a letter for a christening.” When he return, Tiger ask him the name of the chile. He says the name is “Top take off.” Another week came again. He say receive another letter for another christening. After he come back, Tiger ask him what’s the name of the chile again. He says, “Catch in de middle.” An’ the las’ week he went back for another christening. Tiger ask him when he come back what’s the name of the chile. He says, “Lick clean.”

          Now he says, “Tiger, let us go look for this keg of butter.” He carried Tiger all over the place walkin’ until he get tired, an’ when he nearly catch to the place where they hid the butter he said, “Tiger, we are tired, let us go for a sleep!” An’ after Tiger was sleeping, he went to the keg, he took a bit of stick an’ he scrape as much as he can get from the keg, an’ he wipe a little on Tiger mouth an’ he wipe a little at the tail. Then he climb a tall tree now and he make a wonderful alarm that Tiger eat butter until he melt butter!

          Tacoomah’s Corn-piece.

          Anansi’s music gives instructions while providing him with an alibi.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Adolphus Iron, Claremont, St. Ann.

          Reading note: Crop theft and a death.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Tacoomah plant a piece of corn. When it commence to dry, den begin to t’ief it. Tacoomah charge Hanansi. Hanansi say, “Brar, no me!” By dis time Hanansi was a fiddler. Hanansi tell Tacoomah say, “Brar, you say me broke you’ corn, you mek one dance an’ get me fe play.” Tacoomah say yes. De night of de dance, Hanansi get one gang tell dem say, “As you hear me begin play, you start a-brekkin’.” De tune Hanansi play was dis fe de whole night:

          “Two two grain, broke dem go ’long,

          Eb’rybody broke, broke dem go ’long,

          Green an’ dry, broke dem go ’long.”

          In de morning when de dance finish, Tacoomah go down a him cornpiece. Him holla out, “Lawd! Brar Nansi, come heah! not one lef’.” Hanansi turn ’roun’ say, “T’ink you say a me a t’ief you corn. Las’ night you no get me fe play a you dance? den if dem broke out you corn, how you say a me?” Tacoomah tak it to heart an’ drop down dead.

          The Rain.

          A goat uses transformation and another animal’s help to escape.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Richard Pottinger, Claremont, St. Ann.

          Reading note: Threat of being eaten.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Anansi and Goat have a little quarrel. Anansi said to Goat, “Brar Goat, I gwine ketch you!” Goat say, “You never live, me frien’, to ketch me!” Goat ’fraid fe rain. So one moist night Goat was coming from his field had to pass Anansi’s house, drizzle drizzle rain fall; Brar Goat have to run up Anansi’s house.—“Come in, me frien’!” Goat go in. Anansi step in a room tak out him fiddle:—

          “Me t’ank Brar Rain

          Fe run wil’ meat from bush

          Come a house.”

          Goat didn’t like it, keep to de door-way. Anansi not notice him, only playing de same song. Goat jump down de bottom door Anansi cut after him. Goat can’t cross river, run to de river-side turn a white little stone. Dog see, de odder side of de river, when Goat turned a little stone. Anansi run up de river now.—“Brar Dog, see Brar Goat pass?”—“Yes, Brar! see one little stone a river-side deh? takee up t’rowee, I show you whe’ him deh.” Anansi tak up de stone, t’row it de odder side, give Brar Dog. Goat drop on him four feet. Anansi say, “Luck in me han’ an’ it get ’way!”

          Turtle fool Anansi one day. Anansi go out one day an’ him catch one turtle,—quite glad of de turtle! So when he go home, Turtle know Anansi gwine eat him an’ said to Anansi, “Brar Anansi, you know me fat?           Quit-quit and Anansi.

          Two versions let music, food and rivalry change who wins attention.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: David Roach, Lacovia. / Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland.

          Reading note: Rivalry, humiliation and nudity.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Version a: Tailors and Fiddlers

          David Roach, Lacovia.

          Anansi and Lizard go to a ball. Anansi is a fiddler, Lizard is a tailor. Quit-quit was the fiddler. Anansi was playing, “tum, tum, tum” and all the girls were going round Brar Quit-quit. So Anansi play, “Me nyam-nyam taya!” an’ it please the people. All love taya; all the girls crowded round Brar Anansi. Brar Quit-quit says, “Taya no somet’ing!” Then Anansi comes in with his music—“Me nyam de somet’ing! If taya no somet’ing, whe’ are de somet’ing?”

          Brar Anansi said mus’ mak a suit of clo’es for him that kyan’t match. Brar Quit-quit tell him mus’ mak a suit out of maggot-fly. An’ after the ball they went to dinner an’ when the maggot-fly smell the meat, they run off leave him naked.

          Version b: Fiddlers

          Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland.

          Anansi and Tiger bot’ of dem are fiddler an’ go play fe de king ball. So Tiger could play more dan Anansi. So de king say de man could play de best would get married to de king daughter. Dem had dinner after de ball, so after dem play, play, play, Anansi find Tiger playing more dan him, so de lady more cleave to Tiger. So Anansi whisper to Tiger, say Tiger mus’ play,

          Nyam nyam no not’ing!

          As he commence play, de lady say de meaning “Belly-feed no not’ing, but mus’ somet’ing!” So Anansi set him fiddle, play,

          Bittle no somet’ing, what is somet’ing?

          De lady cleave to Anansi an’ drive away Tiger.

          Look again

          Compare David Roach’s version from Lacovia with Henry Spence’s from Bog. Do not merge them into one teller.

          Why Tumble-bug Rolls in the Dung.

          Swapped jars turn a marriage competition into an animal explanation.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: William Forbes, Dry River, Cock-pit country.

          Reading note: Dung, theft and humiliation.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Deh was Mr. Anansi and Tumble-bug. Deh was a young lady, was de king daughter. Her fader said who come wid a jar of money will get dat young lady to marry. Tumble-bug get a jar of money. Anansi get a jar an’ couldn’t get no money to put in it, get some cow dung an’ some horse dung fill up de jar. And after dem was going up to de young lady, dem ketch to a shop. And de two jar favor one anodder. An’ Anansi said, “Brar Tumble-bug, let we go in de shop go get a drink.” An’ Anansi said, “Mus’ buy a bread come,” an’ as he come out, him tak up Tumble-bug jar and lef’ fe him jar. An’ Tumble-bug tak up Anansi jar. And when dem go up to de young lady in de king yard, Anansi said, “Massa, mus’ bring a clean sheet go t’row out money out of jar!” An’ he t’row out money—wa-a-a-a-a! An’ as Tumble-bug t’row, him t’row out horse-dung an’ cow-dung.

          Anansi said, “Tak it up, tak it up, tak it up, you nasty fellow, carry out de missis yard!” Dat is why you see Tumble-bug roll in filth to-day to-day.

          Why Dog is always Looking.

          Anansi’s description of a yam harvest depends on a change of scale.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Moses Hendricks, Mandeville.

          Reading note: Deception about land and food.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Anansi and Dog were friends. They wanted to go into cultivation, so both of them went out in search of good lands to rent. They came across a nice bit of land. Anansi fell in love with the spot; Dog fell in love with the spot too. Anansi said to Dog he remembered when he was a little boy his father planted yams on that very spot of land,—“An’ the yams did bear.” Dog said, “How they bear big?” Anansi said, “Brar Dog, they bear big, they bear big like me leg!” (Anansi’s leg is jus’ like a thread!) Brar Dog say, “Before I work an’ plant yam, an’ the yam not bigger than you leg, I sooner walk round an’ look!” That’s the reason why, when you’re eating, a dog ’sure to be looking at you.

          Anansi was gwine out one day an’ he stop a ribber-side a-eatin’. A rock-stone beg him, an’ wouldn’t gi’ him none. After eat done, wan’ to get up; rock-stone hol’ him an’ he couldn’t get up. An’ began to bawl. A man was coming pas’ same time an’ ask him, “Bredder Anansi, who been a cry heah?” Anansi said, “Don’ know!” An’ de man go inside de bush, go hide.           One man got a darter. He said, “Got one cotton tree; de man cut dat cotton tree, he marry to me darter.” Every man go cut, soon dey cut de chip fasten back; so dem couldn’t get de girl to marry. Toad said him go fall him. Toad full in pocket a hashes an’ every chop him chop him fling de hashes upon de tree when de chip fly, and ’ey kyan’t fasten. So Toad do an’ do till he fell de cotton tree.

          De master hab a long barbecue an’ tell him say, “Now you mus’ go down dere and ’trip yo’self an’ I wi’ pour on de water to let you skin.” All dis time one big pot hot water on de fire boil up, so dem turn over de pot o’ hot water an’ say, “Brar Toad, water come! tak you rubbin’ clot’.” An’ Toad jump in wild pine; up to dis day, ev’ry night you hear him cry out, “Kwoka soaka!”

          Rat got married, an’ dere was rice and peas provide for de helping of food fe de dinner. It was so richly cook an’ so much dat it get burn. So Rat remember dat de rice burn in de pot, an’ Rat like ’crapin’, an’ while he was goin’ home wid his wife in de way, when he get part way he said to her, “I forget somet’ing very valuable in de wedding house, have to go back fe it!” She said yes, an’ put out de buggy on de water-table an’ run back to de wedding house, never went in where everybody in de house merrying himself, went to de kitchen. So de pot wid de bu’n rice was lean up by de side of de wall. So de force he go to de pot wid trouble de pot, an’ de pot, ’stead of rolling away, tu’n over cover him underneat’. An’ when he fin’ dat he couldn’t come out, he said, “Chut! what about dat? I wouldn’t give a biscuit fe a man who kyan’t lose his night rest!” and he begin to ’crape bu’nt part kur-ur-rup krup krup krup.

          His wife calling now, “Mr. Rat! Mr. Rat!”—“Me head fasten in pot o!” Tu’n back ’crape ’crape. So de cook hear de noise and went out in de kitchen, find it was Rat underneat’ de pot an’ call out fe help. An’ come out lift up de pot an’ kill him. Dat’s why so many widows in de world, because dere husband died and left ’em.

          Settling the Father’s Debt.

          A child’s riddling explanations become payment of a family debt.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains.

          Reading note: A dying child, parasites and household debt.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          A man owe another one five pounds, and the other called in and asked the son who was at home, “Where is your father?”—“Me father gone to break a new fence to mend a rotten one.”—“Where is your mother?”—“Me mother gone to the market to sell sweet to buy sweet.”—“Where is your older brother?”—“Gone to sea to catch what in catching will kill and what him don’ catch will carry home alive.”—“Where is your sister?”—“Me sister in the house weeping over what she was rejoicing about last year.”—“What are you doing?”—“Taking hot bricks out of oven.”—“Now, me good boy, you give me some hard puzzle. If you tell me the meaning I’ll give you five pounds.”—“When I tell you me father gone to break a new fence to mend an old one, mean to say me father owe you five pound and gone to borrow five pound to pay you. When I tell you me mother gone to the market to sell sweet to buy sweet, gone to sell honey to buy sugar. When I said me brother gone to the sea to catch what in catching he kill and what him don’ catch him bring home alive, I mean to say he goes to bed and he will catch the lice from his head and kill them; what he don’ catch he mus’ carry back in the head. When I said me sister was in the house weeping over what she was rejoicing over last year, she was rejoicing last year in getting her baby; she is weeping over it now because it is dying. When I tell you I’m taking hot bricks out of oven, I am pulling chiggers out of me feet.”—“Now all your puzzles are put through, you are worthy of the five pounds.”—“Please settle me father’s debt, then.” So he make a receipt and give his father five pounds.

          The Tree-wife.

          A tree becomes a wife; a song follows a trail of answers.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Thomas White, Maroon Town.

          Reading note: Magical marriage, nakedness and a disputed household relationship.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          It was a man didn’t have no wife an’ he was a hunter-man; he hunt in de bush all day. An’ one day he go in de bush, go an’ shoot, an’ when he coming home, him saw a pretty tree name of Jessamy, an’ he say, “O me biddy boy, das a pretty tree!” An’ he says, “If dis tree could tu’n a wife to me, I would like to be marry to him!” An’ so he said, it done de very same as what him said; de tree do tu’n a wife for him. De woman was naked, an’ he lef’ him at de said time an’ went home back, an’ he get some clot’ing for de woman, an’ got him dress up nicely an’ carry him home at house.

          An’ deh he an’ de woman was fo’ a long time until one day he were gwine out a bush fe gwine shoot, an’ leave him wife a house. Him go an’ sleep an’ never come home till de nex’ day. An’ after he gone to de wood, it’s anudder man go dere an’ inveigle him wife an’ tek’ him away from him house an’ go to dis man house. An’ when de poor man come home from bush de nex’ day, he couldn’t fin’ him wife. An’ what de wife did, after de wife come out dis man’s house go to de nex’ house, she was frighten how him husban’ gwine fin’ him. An’ de nex’ man house about a two mile off him husban’ house, an’ as she leaving for him house, she spit all de way until she ketch to dis odder man’s house.

          An’ de man was into a rage dat him couldn’t fin’ him wife an’ didn’t know what was to ever do. An’ him sing,

          Jesta be-yo, eh-e-eh-eh-eh-o—— Jesta be-yo, A, a wi’ die, oh, wi’a go die, oh, fe trees bear-e, oh, A, a wi’ die, oh, wi a go die, oh, fe trees bear-e, oh.

          When de man sing, de spit dat de woman spit answer him,—

          “Jesta be-yo, eh, eh, eh, o!

          Jesta be-yo, a wi’ die-o,

          Wi’ a go die-o, fe trees bear-e o!”

          To every place where de woman spit, de man go dere an’ stan’ an’ call—

          “Jesta be-yo, eh, eh, eh, o,”

          at each stopping-place of half a mile until two miles are passed. An’ jus’ as de woman hear de voice of de man, stan’ at door-mout’ an’ see dat de man coming. An’ de man go tak him wife an’ catch him right back to home yard.

          Jack man dory, choose none!

          Bird Arinto.

          David Lawrence defeats a bird; Anansi claims the achievement.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Mrs. Ramtalli, Maggotty.

          Reading note: A flesh-eating bird, abandonment and killing.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          There was a bird Arinto; it used to feed on human flesh. In the district there was a little boy by the name of David Lawrence who was lame in both feet. When the boy heard the bird fly, he asked his sister to take him; but she refused, saying if she remained Arinto would eat her too. The boy, having no other resource, dug a hole in the ground where he lived for some time. When the bird came and perched on the house-top, he said, “Smell flesh; somebody about here!” Then David Lawrence sang,

          ♩ = 108

          You Arintoe, You Arintoe, Shake, shake, come down to David Lawrence.

          Then the bird pitched off the house to the spot where he heard the singing. As it was an underground passage, the boy would move along and the bird would follow him up and down. As he went to the foot (of the passage), the bird would go there; as he went above, the bird would go there,—all day like that. At night the bird would go to rest,—couldn’t eat he was so tired. But the boy cooked at night and had his rest.

          It went on for some weeks until the bird got tired an’ weary and one night fell off the roost. David Lawrence came out, cut out the tongue, and took it to the king, who had promised whoever killed Arinto would get his daughter’s hand in marriage. Anansi, passing the nex’ day, saw the dead bird, cut off the head and hurried with it to the king. A wedding feast was made to have Anansi married to (the king’s) daughter. Just as that was going on, a ragged boy called at the gate, but Anansi told the king to have nothing to do with him. But he appealed so loudly that the king after all went out, and the boy said to him, “Anansi is a usurper, because, king, have you ever seen a head without a tongue?” Anansi, on hearing that, ran under the table and from there into the house-top. David Lawrence was taken in, dressed, married to the king’s daughter, and lived happily.

          Jack man dora!

Anansi say he mus’ get that money. Now he went an’ mak a bargain with Mosquito that Mosquito mus’ go in the girl room, as he’s a small man an’ can go thru crevices, an’ he, Anansi will go underneath the mother room. In the night while the girl was sleeping, Mosquito went an’ sing at her ear; an’ the girl then knock her han’ up on Mosquito an’ say, “Go ’way!” At that time the mother stop into her room an’ hear. After a little time, Mosquito went back to the girl ear an’ sing again. The girl knock after him an’ say, “Go ’way!” again. Anansi underneath the mother’s room give a clear listening. A little time after, Mosquito went back to the girl an’ sing at her ear. She then knock after him again an’ say, “Go ’way!” The mother then called to the girl, said, “Zegrady, Zegrady, what’s the matter?” The daughter said, “It is something worrying me in my sleep, mum.” Anansi never wait now for Mosquito, run right to his house, take up his fiddle an’ begin to play,—

          “Zegrady, Zegrady, Zegra, Zegrady,

          Come shake up Anansi hand,

          My dear!”

          The next morning he start for the house and play. So the girl hear her name and say, “Mother, I heard someone call my name!” So the old woman invite Anansi to come in an’ Anansi get the money, never give Mosquito none. So from that day is why Mosquito flying at people ear making noise, because Anansi rob him out of the money.

          Look again

          If a story has a winner, is that the same thing as a hero?

          JAMAICAN STORYTELLING · HISTORICAL SOURCE

          The Water Crayfish.

          A found child returns to the river and reveals another identity.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Moses Hendricks, Mandeville.

          Reading note: A child is hit; a magical child leaves a household.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          There was a wealthy woman, but she had no children. She was always wishful of adopting a child. So she went down to the river to bathe one morning as usual and she saw a pretty baby. She was so glad she took it home and she made a pet of it. She employed a girl called Tamanty to care for the child, and Anansi to be the watchman to watch and see if the girl cared for the child.

          So it happened one day she had to go out, so she left them to take care of the child. Anansi wanted all along to get rid of this girl Tamanty. Tamanty was sweeping the house and the little child was playing with the broom. Anansi winked to the girl and said, “Lick him wi’ the broomstick! lick him wi’ the broomstick!” The girl took the broomstick and hit the child. The child started running for the river. Anansi and Tamanty started after her, calling out, “Come back, Miss Nancy, come back!” The child said,

          “No na no, Tamanty! no na no, Anansi!

          Me a river craw-fish, me no have a mu-ma,

          Poor me, river craw-fish! river a me mu-ma.”

          The child ran right into the river and became a cray-fish.

          Look again

          What does the song reveal that the adopting household did not understand?

          JAMAICAN STORYTELLING · HISTORICAL SOURCE

          Robin as Fortune-teller.

          Accidental remarks make Robin look like a successful fortune-teller.

          ← Written talesJamaican voices →

          Teller and place: Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland.

          Reading note: Animals killed for food and a false claim to special knowledge.

          Edition: collected during Beckwith’s 1919/1921 visits; published 1924. Historical transcription, not a newly composed retelling. Narrative wording and printed song words retained; page and reference markers removed. This text is not a transcript of the modern performances in the listening room.

          Robin fawn himself to be fortune-teller. So he bet a lot of money dat whatever dey have fe dinner to-night, him will tell it. So Robin name Fox,—call him “Mr. Fox Robin,”—an’ dey didn’t know his name. So it was a fox underneat’ de dish fe de dinner. So when him come in, frighten’, t’ink him goin’ to lose, him sit down, say, “Aye, poor Fox is caught to-day!” When dey hear him say dis, everybody give a shout. Him win; for it was a fox underneat’ de dish.

          Once de good man again go out to shoot. So him coming home, hear about Fox too,—same Fox. So him catch a robin redbreast an’ kill it an’ roast it an’ put it under de dish de very same as dey do de fox. So at dinner when he come to a certain time, say, “I want to know what underneat’ de dish now, Mr. Fox?” So said, “Well, poor Robin is well caught to-day!”

          Look again

          What do listeners think they have heard, and what was actually being said?

          JAMAICA, RECONSIDERED · 1 OF 14 · CORRECTION

          Emancipation paid the enslavers. Freedom still had conditions.

          The compensation ledger and James Williams’s account tell a harder story than a date on a national timeline: legal abolition, unpaid labour and the distribution of money were different events.

          ← All 14 essaysRead in sequence →

          The claim under examination

          “Abolition in 1834 immediately freed the enslaved, and compensation repaired their loss.”

          What the evidence changes: The compensation scheme paid people claiming property in the enslaved. Many of the people legally emancipated were compelled into apprenticeship before full freedom in 1838.

          The celebration needs more than one date

          A timeline can make emancipation look like a door opened once. It is more accurate to ask which door opened, for whom, and what stood on the other side. The abolition of the British slave trade in 1807 was not the abolition of slavery. The 1833 legislation took effect in 1834, while compulsory apprenticeship extended unfreedom for many people in Jamaica until 1838. Ending lawful ownership of a person mattered enormously. It did not instantly give that person control of working time, land or the terms on which a family could survive. [4]

          The original statute’s emancipating language and the apprentice’s account should therefore be read together. The law announces a change in legal status. Williams describes encounters with employers, magistrates and punishment after that change. These sources answer different questions, and that difference is the opening into a better history. The gap between them is not solved by choosing whichever source makes the most uplifting anniversary speech. [6]

          Follow the money to the actual beneficiary

          Britain’s compensation package was £20 million for enslavers’ claimed loss of property. It was not a payment to the people who had been enslaved. UCL’s research makes that asymmetry central to the record it reconstructs. Money attached to a property claim tells us what the settlement recognized as compensable; the labour and suffering of the person classified as property were not rewarded by that scheme. The distinction is a fact about the scheme, not a claim that emancipation itself was meaningless. [5]

          Anson and Bennett show another layer: intermediaries could profit by collecting awards and charging commissions. Their investigation of government stock follows a specific financial dataset, including awards associated with colonies outside Jamaica. We should not turn its sample into Jamaica’s compensation total. Its larger lesson is that the money moved through institutions and agents. A list of proprietors is only the beginning of the financial history. [3]

          Three events to keep separate

          1807
          Abolition of the British slave trade; existing slavery continued.
          1834
          The abolition settlement took effect; apprenticeship restricted many emancipated people’s labour.
          1838
          Full emancipation in Jamaica; neither land redistribution nor equality automatically followed.

          This is a sequence of legal changes, not a measure of how free every household felt.

          Let an apprentice interrupt the official story

          The title page is already an argument: a narrative beginning with the first of August 1834, written in the name of an “apprenticed labourer.” Williams locates his upbringing at Penshurst in St. Ann. His opening comparison is blunt: he reports worse punishment under the new system and recounts being brought before magistrates. The text names places and people. It gives the reader concrete proceedings to examine rather than an abstract assurance that a new legal label brought humane treatment. [1]

          Williams’s account is testimony, not a transparent recording. Duke’s account of Paton’s edition places the printed narrative within the transatlantic anti-apprenticeship campaign. That makes the mediation important, but it does not justify discarding the speaker. Ask how the narrative was produced, what can be corroborated, and what the account permits us to say about a particular encounter. The existence of an abolitionist publishing network is part of the history of how his words reached readers. [2]

          Paton’s scholarly edition emphasizes the connection between punitive legal machinery and apprenticeship. A proprietor’s inability to punish in precisely the old way did not prevent pressure through a magistrate or workhouse. That is a more revealing question than whether apprenticeship was “really slavery” in a slogan’s sense. What powers changed hands? Which constraints continued? Where could a worker challenge an accusation, and at what cost? [2]

          A monumental hero and a small printed page

          A monument and a pamphlet can be read without placing them in competition. The monument helps preserve the importance of collective struggle. The pamphlet demands attention to the terms of the settlement that followed. Freedom’s history needs both public memory and the administrative details through which people were compelled, fined, imprisoned or paid. The smaller object can change the interpretation of the larger landmark.

          What this correction does not erase

          This argument does not deny the work of abolitionists or the significance of legal emancipation. Walvin’s account places abolition within Britain’s long involvement in slavery rather than allowing the story of its ending to replace the history of its operation. The guide’s conclusion is that the celebration becomes more informed when we follow beneficiaries and burdens alongside legislation. A heroic conclusion is too short if it leaves the apprentice standing at the workhouse door. [4]

          Nor does a compensation award, by itself, prove the entire later history of a family’s wealth. That requires tracing debts, inheritance, purchases and institutions. The award is evidence of a transaction and a recognized interest. Use it as a research starting point, not permission to invent a complete financial biography. This matters when local estate stories connect to people and organisations elsewhere.

          Put the evidence to work

          Compare the title page with the compensation research. Write down whose loss the money recognized, whose labour remained constrained, and which source establishes each answer. Then read one named episode in Williams rather than treating his whole account as an interchangeable “slave narrative.”

          Tony’s Call Celebrate emancipation with the ledger and the apprentice in view. A date tells us when the law changed; it does not tell us who received the money or who controlled the next working day.

          Scholarship and evidence

          2. Paton, D. (Ed.). (2001). A Narrative of Events … by James Williams, an Apprenticed Labourer in Jamaica. Duke University Press. Scholarly edited edition; publisher account consulted, not the full modern introduction. ↩
          3. Anson, M., & Bennett, M. D. (2022). The collection of slavery compensation, 1835–43. Bank of England Staff Working Paper 1,006. Research summary consulted; its financial sample is not a Jamaica-only total. ↩
          4. Walvin, J. (2007). Abolishing the slave trade. Institute of Historical Research, History in Focus. Historian’s essay consulted: abolition’s place in a longer British history of slavery. ↩
          5. UCL. Legacies of British Slavery. Made at UCL. Research project account consulted. Modern-value estimates are deliberately not repeated here. ↩

          JAMAICA, RECONSIDERED · 2 OF 14 · COMPLICATION

          The Maroon treaty secured freedom—and obligations to slavery.

          A hard-won settlement protected a community. Its clauses also required the return of future fugitives and help against rebellion. Read those provisions together before turning Maroon history into either a spotless victory or a simple betrayal.

          ← All 14 essaysRead in sequence →

          The claim under examination

          “The treaty was an uncomplicated victory for the freedom of all enslaved Jamaicans.”

          What the evidence changes: Cudjoe’s agreement protected named communities within a colonial order that continued to enslave others. Freedom, land, commercial permission and coercive obligations coexist in the document.

          The victory was real. Read whom it covered.

          The second article promises liberty to Cudjoe, his captains and people, while addressing people who had recently joined them in a more qualified way. The third specifies land. Those were consequential gains wrested from a colonial power after sustained conflict. But a promise to particular communities is not a promise to every enslaved person in Jamaica. The distinction lies in the wording of the settlement, not in a modern effort to diminish resistance. [1]

          The agreement reproduced by the Assembly carries the date 1 March 1738–9. The paired year reflects historical dating practice; it should not be silently converted into a different festival date. The text reproduced here is Cudjoe’s western settlement. It cannot stand in for every eastern agreement or every Maroon community’s history. Local specificity is the first protection against an islandwide myth built from a single document.

          The clause that an uncomplicated victory cannot absorb

          Article nine · read the obligation

          “That if any negroes shall hereafter run away from their masters or owners, and fall into Captain Cudjoe’s hands, they shall immediately be sent back to the Chief Magistrate of the next parish where they are taken; and those that bring them are to be satisfied for their trouble, as the legislature shall appoint.”

          Historical classification retained from the 1739 agreement. This clause concerns future runaways; article two and article ten address other categories. Examine the full primary transcription ↗

          The confirming statute gives the arrangement an administrative mechanism: the magistrate was to pay ten shillings for a fugitive delivered by Cudjoe or people under his command and arrange onward custody. The exact payment is in section II of the act, not the literal wording of article nine. That distinction matters because a paraphrase can make a correct general point while misrepresenting where the evidence sits. [1]

          Article six adds an obligation to assist in suppressing rebels, with a qualification concerning acceptance of the settlement’s terms. Article seven concerns defence against foreign invasion. Read together, the provisions connect Maroon security to services valuable to the colony. The colonial government did not simply accept an independent refuge and disappear. It sought an organised relationship with communities it had been unable to eliminate.

          Land and commerce were regulated, too

          Article four permits agriculture, stock raising and sale of produce while requiring a magistrate’s licence when commodities are brought to market. Later clauses concern roads, annual appearances when required, resident white intermediaries and succession. The text therefore tells a story of negotiated room to live and limits on that room. Counting only the acres misses the network of obligations surrounding the land. [1]

          The guide’s interpretation is that this was a settlement of power, not a modern declaration of universal human rights. The people negotiating wanted survival, security and recognized space for their descendants. The colony wanted peace and assistance in maintaining order. Those interests overlapped in places and conflicted in others. That structure helps explain the document without making each party’s motive identical.

          Scholarship goes beyond the two familiar verdicts

          McKee’s article shifts attention from an exclusive story of resistance or betrayal to interactions and alliances between Maroons and nearby white settlers. Its stated scope is 1739–1795. Siva’s thesis abstract likewise examines post-treaty social, economic and demographic history and highlights policing obligations. These research questions are useful because a treaty starts a relationship; it does not end history. Implementation, trade, disputes and internal change remain to be studied. [2]

          The distinction between obligation and practice is essential. A clause establishes what the agreement required. It does not, alone, tell us how frequently it was enforced, whether every captain behaved alike, or how every enslaved person encountered Maroons. Siva’s wider historical project points toward those questions. We should not calculate a record of all fugitive returns from one paragraph of legal text. [3]

          A living community is not a colonial contract

          UNESCO’s account of the Blue and John Crow Mountains emphasizes refuge, trails, spiritual connections and living Maroon heritage, including Moore Town. That complements the legal text without making the western agreement a description of all eastern practices. Contemporary community knowledge, ritual and land relations require their own identified evidence. A person living now should not be reduced to the most troubling provision in an eighteenth-century agreement. [4]

          The named Moore Town and Accompong performances on Drums of Defiance supply another kind of record. They document artists and occasions, not the negotiations themselves. Hearing cultural continuity is valuable; using a twentieth-century performance to prove what was sung in 1739 would be an unsupported leap. The article links the guide’s listening resources so the legal and cultural histories can be studied together. [5]

          Put the evidence to work

          Choose one clause securing freedom, one regulating commerce and one obliging coercive service. Explain who benefits and who bears a constraint in each. Then identify a question the clauses cannot answer without later records. Read all fifteen clauses in the guide →

          Tony’s Call Respect the achievement enough to read its terms. A freedom story that omits article nine is incomplete; a betrayal story that erases the struggle and the living communities is incomplete as well.

          JAMAICA, RECONSIDERED · 3 OF 14 · MISSING HISTORY

          The economy enslaved Jamaicans built beyond the cane fields.

          Provision grounds, markets and locally made pottery reveal knowledge, production and trade that a plantation-only picture leaves out. They also expose the uncomfortable fact that enslavers could benefit from the work people did to keep themselves alive.

          ← All 14 essaysRead in sequence →

          The claim under examination

          “Enslaved Jamaicans appear in economic history only as labour supplied to plantations.”

          What the evidence changes: They also grew food, made goods and participated in exchange networks. The room they created for themselves remained entangled with slavery’s demands and costs.

          The plantation account has a blind spot

          If the history contains only cane, sugar, estate owners and export tonnage, enslaved people enter it as a labour input. That account describes an important coercive industry. It leaves out the practical work of producing meals, tools, vessels and relationships. The omission matters because survival was not provided automatically by the system that demanded labour. A household’s struggle to reproduce itself belongs inside economic history, rather than in a decorative paragraph about customs.

          Edwards, Plummer and McKenzie examine provision grounds across a long Jamaican history. Their article stresses a contradiction: cultivation could sustain foodways and create room for independent action while also reducing the proprietor’s feeding costs. They distinguish survival and resistance from an imagined space wholly outside plantation power. The useful surprise is not that a slave system secretly allowed freedom. It is that people exercised knowledge and initiative inside conditions designed to exploit them. [1]

          A provision ground is not a gift of leisure

          The term may sound modest, but it names a relationship among land, time, food and power. Where a household could cultivate, how far it travelled, and when it could work shaped what growing food required. The garden cannot be understood by counting crops alone. The labour demanded on the estate and the labour needed to keep a family alive occupied the same person’s finite day. A plot could support autonomy and impose another burden at once.

          In this reading, selling a surplus can change a household’s options without ending its subjection. Money from a crop might support a purchase, a relationship or a plan. It did not dissolve the legal claims and punishments surrounding the seller. We should therefore avoid two errors: erasing initiative because slavery was coercive, and making initiative an excuse to soften the coercion. Both elements belong in the same account.

          Pots let us investigate connections that a ledger misses

          Hauser, Descantes and Glascock study locally produced coarse earthenware through compositional analysis. They examine how materials recovered in different contexts can inform the scale and organisation of production and exchange. Their conclusion challenges an initial assumption of only small, household-level production with intermittent distribution: the scale appeared larger than anticipated, while the authors do not claim a simple final answer to every route or production centre. That qualification is part of the finding. [2]

          The method changes the question. Instead of beginning with a proprietor’s list of transactions, it starts with things used, broken, discarded and recovered. Similarities and differences in the materials can test whether a story of isolated plantation households is adequate. A ceramic sherd becomes evidence of technical practice and a possible connection. It does not give us the potter’s name, a complete trading itinerary or a photograph of the exchange.

          The paper also relates pottery knowledge to women’s production and transmission, drawing on ethnographic evidence. This connects craft with social networks rather than treating a vessel as a timeless African survival. The analytical move is important: continuity must be investigated through practice, context and evidence. A shape that looks familiar does not automatically prove an uninterrupted tradition or identify a particular maker’s birthplace. [2]

          An evidence chain, not a romantic reconstruction

          1. Object: locally made pottery recovered in a recorded archaeological context.
          2. Method: compare composition, manufacture and distribution.
          3. Inference: test possible production and exchange networks.
          4. Limit: do not invent an individual potter, sale or journey from a fragment.

          Examine the paper’s object photographs and analysis ↗

          The garden and the great house were in the same economy

          Place the estate photograph beside the market photograph. One invites attention to an export-producing landscape; the other to circulation among many sellers and buyers. Neither can establish the eighteenth-century network on its own, but together they suggest why a history organised only around the great house is incomplete. Ask where people grew food, stored it, carried it, prepared it and sold it. Those tasks connect the landscape differently.

          Emancipation did not create economic life from nothing

          The National Library’s free-village account describes purchases of land and lots in the transition after emancipation. That settlement history should be read alongside the research on earlier production and exchange. The guide’s interpretation is that freed people were not blank economic subjects suddenly supplied with initiative. They entered a new legal situation with accumulated knowledge and relationships, while access to land and control of labour remained contested. [5]

          Mintz and Hall’s 1960 study is an important entry in the research tradition on Jamaica’s internal markets; the author’s bibliography establishes that publication. It is offered as further reading here, not as an excuse to attach a famous name to claims from a book we have not independently inspected. The case made in this essay rests on the specific articles and evidence identified above. [4]

          Hear the market as a problem, not just a tune

          Louise Bennett’s Linstead Market performance supplies another way into the subject: a vendor’s account of disappointing trade is culturally meaningful even though the recording is later than the photographs and much later than slavery. The song is not a census or a financial return. Its value is to bring the work and uncertainty of selling into the listening session. Hear the identified performance in the guide → [6]

          Put the evidence to work

          Compare an estate-centred explanation with the pottery evidence. List one activity each source makes visible and one it leaves out. Explain how a provision ground could support a household and benefit an enslaver at the same time, without making those benefits equal.

          Tony’s Call Put the food grower, trader and potter back into the economic story. Their knowledge mattered before emancipation, and recognising it should make the account of exploitation sharper.

          Scholarship and evidence

          JAMAICA, RECONSIDERED · 4 OF 14 · SCHOLARLY REINTERPRETATION

          Morant Bay: an inquiry could condemn brutality and narrow justice.

          Paul Bogle’s rebellion challenged land, taxation, representation and colonial power. Jonathan Connolly’s research shows how the official inquiry and legal controversy redirected that larger argument into questions about the governor’s authority.

          ← All 14 essaysRead in sequence →

          The claim under examination

          “The inquiry into Morant Bay simply established the truth and restored impartial British justice.”

          What the evidence changes: Inquiry produced important evidence and criticism, but also shaped what counted as relevant. Connolly argues that legal proceedings displaced a systemic challenge to colonial rule and helped legitimate more centralised imperial control.

          Begin before the courthouse burned

          On 11 October 1865, protesters approached the courthouse at Morant Bay. Connolly places the attempted arrest of Bogle within a wider history of poverty, taxation, restricted representation and a legal system dominated by planter interests. The event did become violent. But reducing it to a spontaneous eruption of disorder discards the political claims made before and around that violence. A crowd has a history, not merely a headcount. [1]

          The “Underhill meetings,” petitions and public arguments discussed in the article are important because they show Jamaicans interpreting their own situation. Their complaints concerned how colonial policy constrained life after slavery. The issue was not simply whether a benevolent authority would hear a request more kindly. It was whether freedom could have substance when land, taxation and political power remained arranged against the labouring population.

          The Queen’s advice was not an economically neutral answer

          Connolly examines a dispatch known as the “Queen’s Advice,” drafted by the Colonial Office and circulated by Governor Eyre. It rejected the assessment of deep colonial poverty and emphasized wage labour. Protesters’ responses questioned the reality of post-slavery freedom. The apparent disagreement over diligence was also a disagreement over the structure of opportunities. Who controlled land? Who bore taxes? Who decided that the worker’s circumstances were the worker’s own fault? [1]

          Keep the questions visible

          The protesters’ larger questions: land, wages, taxation, representation and the meaning of freedom.

          The later legal focus: martial law, the governor’s authority and individual criminal responsibility.

          These are the guide’s summary of Connolly’s argument, not a facsimile of Bogle’s petition or the commission’s report.

          This is a useful surprise because it changes the starting point of the history. If we begin with the burning courthouse, we are likely to ask only about the restoration of order. If we begin with the preceding petitions and arguments, we can see why the existing order was itself under challenge. That does not excuse every act of the rebellion. It establishes the problem that participants were attempting to address.

          Suppression and investigation were different exercises of power

          The suppression continued under martial law after organised resistance had quickly been put down. Connolly describes killings, flogging and destruction of homes and shows how the royal commission condemned major aspects of that conduct. An inquiry that records and criticizes abuse has real evidentiary value. The harder question is what it makes visible while setting other questions aside. [1]

          He argues that the commission and later proceedings translated a broad critique of colonial society into a narrower dispute over the proper use of executive power. That is an interpretation advanced through detailed documentary analysis, not the only possible definition of the event. It complements earlier scholarship on the rebellion and on British debates over race and martial law. We should state the argument as his, then examine whether the records support it.

          An important campaign could still leave the empire intact

          John Stuart Mill and the Jamaica Committee sought to hold Eyre accountable. Their challenge to arbitrary punishment was consequential; it should not be dismissed as empty theatre. Connolly nonetheless shows how the language of protected imperial subjects could preserve the larger imperial framework. Defending people against abuse and questioning the legitimacy of colonial rule were related projects, but they were not identical. [1]

          The contrast is especially clear in the proceedings against Eyre. Questions of criminal responsibility concerned identifiable actions and lawful authority, not the entire economic organisation that had produced unrest. Legal relevance narrowed the available field. A court could ask whether a governor had exceeded his powers without deciding whether the political economy he administered was unjust. The limits could operate through legal categories even without every participant deliberately trying to silence a grievance.

          What the failed prosecution establishes

          The Middlesex grand jury rejected the indictment in 1868. It is therefore inaccurate to tell this episode as a completed trial and conviction of Eyre. Connolly analyzes Justice Blackburn’s charge as the culminating legal pronouncement because the case did not proceed as the campaigners hoped. Procedural precision matters: an attempted prosecution, instructions to a jury and a conviction are different events with different implications. [1]

          The essay’s conclusion is more unsettling than “Britain corrected a rogue governor.” Investigating the scandal could reposition the problem as poor local governance and support further centralisation of imperial control. In that reading, the system absorbed a challenge by redefining it. The historian’s task is not simply to repeat the commission’s verdict, but to investigate how the verdict altered the story being told.

          A hero’s image should lead us back to the claims

          Bogle’s place as a national hero preserves the importance of his leadership and sacrifice. JIS and JNHT provide routes into that public memory and the surviving courthouse site. The danger comes when a memorial encounter stops at an image and an execution date. A more informed visit asks what people wanted, how they organised, and what the later official narrative did with those demands. [4]

          The earlier history linked below supplies local context; this piece adds a particular scholarly argument about inquiry. Reading the two together helps prevent a new simplification. Connolly’s interpretation does not mean every witness was unheard or every British campaigner insincere. It means that producing an official account is itself a historical act with rules, priorities and consequences.

          Put the evidence to work

          Make two lists: grievances before the uprising, and questions addressed in the Eyre proceedings. Identify a grievance that does not fit easily into a prosecution for misuse of martial law. Explain why condemning unlawful punishment could leave that grievance unresolved.

          Tony’s Call At Morant Bay, read the demands as carefully as the punishment. An inquiry can expose brutality while changing the question the public is invited to ask.

          Scholarship and evidence

Particularly the sections on systemic critique, inquiry, and The Queen v. Eyre. ↩
